<meta>continues from previous page</meta>God, and he commands that He alone be worshipped everywhere.
But the unlearned and those of a [base] nature—to whom, truly, the fate did not proceed from the Lord to obtain gifts, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jove <note>original: "Iouis"; Augustine often uses the Roman name Jupiter/Jove to refer to the supreme deity in a philosophical context</note>—not listening to both gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all gods. Furthermore, they have chosen not only not to pursue the prohibited demons with any hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things through which alone God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, stands in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore Him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through imitation and instruction concerning Him. For instruction purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward Him. Indeed, he <note>Porphyry</note> preached well concerning God the Father and said by what morals He must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the holy is either praised or blamed.

But among Christians, it was only so much, or he so much slanders them as the demons wish—those whom he thinks are gods—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in honor of the gods in theaters and temples, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building is and where the ruin of morals lies. Who, however, said this to him or inspired him, except a diabolical spirit, such a vain and obvious lie: that the demons prohibited from being worshipped by the Hebrews are revered rather than hated by Christians? 

But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped—and the celestial holy angels and powers of God, whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids sacrifice to be made [to others], thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people; and He brought it in very threateningly, saying: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out." <note>Exodus 22:20</note> And lest anyone should think that the command was not to sacrifice to the most wicked and earthly spirits, whom that man <note>Porphyry</note> calls the least or minor ones—since in the Holy Scriptures these are themselves called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the gentiles—which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> clearly placed in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the gentiles are demons." <note>Psalm 96:5</note> Lest anyone, therefore, should think that sacrifice was indeed prohibited to these demons, but permitted to be made to the celestial ones, either all or some of them, He immediately added: "except to the Lord alone"; that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" should believe God to be only one person to whom he thinks sacrifice must be made. That this is not to be understood so is very easily found in the Greek scriptures.

The God of the Hebrews, therefore, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry</note> provides such a great testimony, gave the law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now made famous among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in His law and His prophets? Indeed, not to search for them—for they are not hidden or rare—but to collect those things which are plain and frequent and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that He, the true and supreme God, willed that sacrifice be made to no one at all except to Himself. 

Behold this one thing, spoken briefly, or rather grandly and threateningly, but truthfully, by that God whom the most learned of those [pagans] proclaim as so excellent: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to gods," He says, "shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." Not that He has need of anything, but because it is expedient for us that we should be His. For to Him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: "I have said to the Lord, You are my God, since You have no need of my goods." <note>Psalm 16:2</note> Moreover, we ourselves are His most noble and best sacrifice. This is His City, the mystery of which thing we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, just as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets sounded oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and the nations, from the rising of the sun even to its setting, would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that even pagan philosophers acknowledge the God of the Hebrews, yet they fail to see that this God demands exclusive worship and forbids sacrifice to demons or lesser spirits. He identifies the Christian community and its "spiritual sacrifice" as the true City of God predicted by the prophets.</summary>
<keywords>Monotheism, Sacrifice, Porphyry, Demons, Hebrew Law, Septuagint, City of God, Moral virtue</keywords>
